title: Binary search

story.title: The commit that broke the build
story.summary: Yesterday the build passed and today it fails. Between the two sit hundreds of commits, and building a commit takes ten minutes. You want to find the first commit that fails by testing as few of them as you can.

uses.title: git bisect
uses.body: Git has this exact search built in. You mark one commit as bad and an older one as good, and `git bisect` checks out the commit halfway between them for you to test. Each answer you give halves the range, until it names the first bad commit.

uses.title: Sorted lists in standard libraries
uses.body: Python's `bisect` module and Java's `Arrays.binarySearch` search a sorted list by halving it. `bisect` can also report where a new value belongs, so a list stays sorted as you insert into it.

uses.title: Database indexes
uses.body: A database index keeps its keys in sorted order, so a lookup by key does not read the whole table. The B-tree used by most databases splits many ways instead of two, but each step still throws away most of what remains.

uses.title: The smallest value that passes a test
uses.body: You can also search for an answer instead of an item: the smallest server capacity that handles the traffic, or the smallest size that fits. It works whenever every value below some point fails and every value above it passes, which is the shape of the broken-build history.

whenNot: Binary search needs the data in order, or at least a yes-or-no test that is no on one side and yes on the other. Sorting unsorted data first costs O(n log n), so for a single lookup a plain scan, O(n), is cheaper. It also needs to jump to the middle in O(1), so it does not suit a linked list. If you only look up exact values and the order does not matter, a hash map answers in O(1) on average. And for a handful of items a scan is just as fast and simpler to get right.

outcomes.pick-the-middle: Pick the middle of the range that is still in play
outcomes.discard-half: Discard the half of the range that cannot hold the answer
outcomes.keep-the-boundary: Move `lo` and `hi` without losing the answer or looping forever
outcomes.state-the-invariant: State what stays true on every pass of the search
outcomes.count-the-builds: State the cost of binary search: O(log n) steps

overview.title: Find a spot by halving
overview.caption: [[binary-search]] finds a position in a sorted array by looking at the middle and throwing away the half that cannot hold the answer, again and again. Three pointers keep track: `lo` and `hi` mark the range that is still in play, and `mid` is the cell you look at. The drawing shows a finished search through eight commits: the three pointers ended up on `c6`, the first commit that fails.

the-problem.title: Which commit broke the build?
the-problem.caption: Yesterday the build passed and today it fails, and the commits between them sit in order, oldest first. Every commit before the culprit builds fine and the culprit and every later one fail. Testing one commit takes ten minutes, so checking 1,000 commits from the oldest one takes nearly a week. You need to find the first bad commit with far fewer builds.
the-problem.keyIdea: When every answer on one side is no and on the other side is yes, one test can rule out half of the range.

the-two-ends.title: The range is the whole history
the-two-ends.caption: You put `lo` on `c1`, the oldest commit, and `hi` on `c8`, the newest. You know `c8` fails, so the first bad commit is somewhere from `lo` to `hi`, and so far that is all eight commits.

pick-the-middle.title: Build the middle commit
pick-the-middle.caption: You build the commit halfway through the range. The middle index is `(lo + hi) / 2`, rounded down: indexes 0 and 7 give 3, which is `c4`. The pointer `mid` marks it.

test-the-middle.title: A good build rules out half
test-the-middle.caption: The build of `c4` passes. The history is in order, with passing commits first, so every commit older than `c4` passes too and the first bad commit has to come after `c4`. Four commits are out with one build.
test-the-middle.keyIdea: One build of the middle commit rules out half of the range.

discard-half.title: Move lo past the middle
discard-half.caption: Since `c4` passed, `lo` jumps to the commit after it, `c5`: `lo` becomes `mid + 1`. The new range is `c5` to `c8`, four commits. The new middle is index 4 plus 7 divided by two, rounded down, which is index 5: `c6`.

keep-the-boundary.title: A bad build keeps the middle in the range
keep-the-boundary.caption: The build of `c6` fails. It could be the first bad commit, or an older commit in the range could be. So `hi` moves onto `c6` itself, not before it: `hi` becomes `mid`. The range is now `c5` and `c6`.
keep-the-boundary.keyIdea: After a bad build, `hi` becomes `mid`; after a good build, `lo` becomes `mid + 1`.

the-range-of-two.title: The middle of two rounds down
the-range-of-two.caption: With `lo` on `c5` and `hi` on `c6`, indexes 4 and 5 add up to 9, and half of 9 is 4.5, which rounds down to 4. The middle is `c5`, the commit you have not built yet. Rounding down is also what keeps the search from getting stuck on `c6`, because `mid` is always strictly before `hi` when the range is more than one commit.

the-pointers-meet.title: Stop when lo meets hi
the-pointers-meet.caption: The build of `c5` passes, so `lo` becomes `mid + 1`: it moves to `c6`, and now `lo` and `hi` sit on the same commit. The range holds one commit and `c6` is the answer. It took 3 builds, `c4`, `c6` and `c5`, instead of 6 for a scan from `c1`.

the-invariant.title: The first bad commit stays in the range
the-invariant.caption: On every pass the same thing is true: the first bad commit is somewhere from `lo` to `hi`. This is the [[loop-invariant]] of the search. It starts true because `hi` is on a commit that fails. Every move keeps it true, because you only drop commits that cannot be the answer. And when `lo` meets `hi`, the range has one commit left, so that commit is the answer.
the-invariant.keyIdea: A loop invariant is a fact that is true before and after every pass. If each move keeps it true, the answer cannot be lost.

count-the-builds.title: Each build halves the range
count-the-builds.caption: Every build cuts the range roughly in half, so 1,000 commits take about 10 builds and 1,000,000 commits about 20. Doubling the history adds only one more build. That growth is [[logarithmic-time]]: O(log n). The ten-minute builds of a week-long hunt shrink to under two hours.
count-the-builds.keyIdea: Halving the range on every step costs O(log n): doubling the input adds one step.

look-up-many-reports.title: Next: answer many reports at once
look-up-many-reports.caption: In Practice you write `firstCommitAtOrAfter`. The history is a sorted list of build numbers, and many reports each name a build number. For every report you return the index of the first commit whose build number is at least that number, or the length of the history when there is none. It is the same search with the test `builds[mid] >= report`, run once per report.

where-you-meet-it.title: Where you will meet it
where-you-meet-it.caption: Here is where halving shows up outside the build server. Some Uses search sorted data and some search for the smallest value that passes a test. The note under them says when to pick something else.

where-the-middle-is.prompt: `lo` is on `c1`, index 0, and `hi` is on `c8`, index 7. The middle index is `(lo + hi) / 2`, rounded down. Select the commit you build first.
where-the-middle-is.explanation: The middle is `c4`. Indexes 0 and 7 add up to 7, half of 7 is 3.5, and rounded down that is index 3, which is `c4`. Choosing `c5` would be rounding up, which breaks the search when the range shrinks to two commits.

where-the-break-can-be.prompt: You build `c4` and it passes. Which commits can still be the first bad one?

options.after-the-middle: Only `c5` to `c8`, because every commit older than a passing one passes too
options.same-side: Only `c1` to `c3`, because the break has to be on the same side as the commit you tested
options.anywhere: Any of `c1` to `c8`, because one passing build says nothing about the other commits
options.right-next-one: Only `c5`, because the first commit after a good one must be the bad one

where-the-break-can-be.explanation: Only `c5` to `c8`. History is ordered, so if `c4` passes then `c1`, `c2` and `c3` pass as well, and the first bad commit comes later. One build does say something about the others, and that is what makes halving work. But it does not pin down `c5`: `c5` could pass too, so the search goes on inside `c5` to `c8`.

where-lo-lands.prompt: `c4` passed, so everything up to `c4` is out. `lo` is still on `c1`. Select the commit `lo` moves to.
where-lo-lands.explanation: `lo` moves to `c5`, the commit right after the middle: `lo` becomes `mid + 1`. `c4` itself passed, so it cannot be the first bad commit, and leaving `lo` on it would keep it in the range for nothing.

where-hi-lands.prompt: `lo` is on `c5` and `mid` is on `c6`. The build of `c6` fails. Where does `hi` go?

options.hi-on-the-middle: Onto `c6` itself, because `c6` could be the first bad commit
options.hi-before-the-middle: Onto `c5`, because `c6` is already known to be bad, so it is no longer needed
options.hi-stays: It stays on `c8`, because a failing build says nothing about the commits after it
options.hi-after-the-middle: Onto `c7`, because the commits after `c6` are the ones left to check

where-hi-lands.explanation: `hi` goes onto `c6`. A failing build does not say that `c6` is the first failing commit, only that the first one is at `c6` or before it, so `c6` has to stay in the range. Moving `hi` to `c5` would throw away the answer when `c6` is the first bad commit. Leaving `hi` on `c8` wastes the build: everything after `c6` is known to fail too, so none of it can be the first bad commit. And `c7` is after `c6`, so it is out, not in.

which-commit-is-built-next.prompt: `lo` is on `c5` and `hi` is on `c6`. Which commit do you build next, and why?

options.rounds-down: `c5`, because the middle of indexes 4 and 5 is 4.5, rounded down to 4
options.rounds-up: `c6`, because with two commits left the middle rounds up to the later one
options.no-build: None, because `c6` already failed, so it must be the first bad commit
options.past-the-end: `c7`, because you have to look one commit past `hi` to be sure

which-commit-is-built-next.explanation: `c5`, because the middle rounds down. `c6` already failed, but that does not make it the first bad commit: `c5` could fail too, and only a build of `c5` can tell. Rounding up would put `mid` on `c6`, which is also `hi`, and the range would never shrink. And `c7` is already out of the range.

why-the-search-stops.prompt: `c5` builds fine, so `lo` moves to `c6`, where `hi` already is. Why can you stop and name the first bad commit?

options.one-candidate-left: Because `lo` and `hi` are on the same commit, so only one commit is left in the range
options.last-one-tested: Because `c5` was the last commit tested, so it is the answer
options.confirm-with-a-build: Because you stop, but you still need one more build of `c6` to confirm it
options.keep-halving: Because a range of one commit cannot be halved, so you have to give up

why-the-search-stops.explanation: Only one commit is left in the range, so `c6` is the answer. You do not need to build `c6` again: `hi` reached it only because its build failed, and every commit before it is out. The last commit you tested is not the answer, because `c5` passed. And a range of one commit is not a failure to halve: it is the point where the invariant names the answer.

builds-for-a-million-commits.prompt: A project has 1,000,000 commits in a row, and the newest one fails. About how many builds does the search need to find the first bad commit?

options.about-twenty: About 20, because every build halves the range and 1,000,000 halved 20 times is down to one
options.about-a-thousand: About 1,000, because halving takes the square root of the number of commits
options.half-a-million: About 500,000, because on average the first bad commit is in the middle
options.a-million: 1,000,000, because in the worst case every commit has to be built

builds-for-a-million-commits.explanation: About 20, because 2 to the power of 20 is just over a million. Each build halves the range, so the cost is O(log n). It does not take the square root: halving shrinks the range much faster than that. The position of the first bad commit does not matter, because every search halves the same way. And a build of every commit is the linear scan the search replaces.

binary-search.gloss: Finding a position in ordered data by testing the middle and discarding the half that cannot hold the answer, until one candidate is left.

loop-invariant.gloss: A fact that is true before a loop starts and after every pass, so it is still true when the loop ends.

logarithmic-time.gloss: Cost that grows by one step each time the input doubles, written O(log n).

exercise.title: Match reports to commits
exercise.task: Write `firstCommitAtOrAfter`, which takes the build numbers of a history, sorted from oldest to newest, and a list of reports, each a build number. For every report return the index of the first commit whose build number is at least the report, or the length of the history when no commit qualifies. Use [[binary-search]] so each report costs O(log n) even on a long history.
hints: The build numbers are sorted, so the commits that are at least the report all sit on the right of the ones that are not. Which index are you looking for?

Keep two indexes, lo and hi, so that the answer is always between them. The answer can be one past the last commit, so think about where hi starts. Look at the middle: should the answer stay at it or move past it?
When the middle commit is at least the report, it could be the answer, so hi becomes mid. Otherwise lo becomes mid plus 1. Stop when lo and hi meet, and do this once per report.
